extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and pragmatic rules for constructing and reading elementary mathematical proofs involving quantifiers, conjunctions, biconditionals, disjunctions, and basic set/number arguments. Focused on what proof steps to perform and how to organize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove universal statements by arbitrary element
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form ∀x P(x), let x be arbitrary and prove P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a fresh arbitrary element of the domain, assume the hypothesis needed (e.g., x∈A when proving A⊆B), and show the property for that arbitrary x. Afterward conclude the universal statement because x was arbitrary. Illustrated repeatedly (e.g., proving A⊆B\C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove existential statements by exhibiting a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form ∃x P(x), provide a specific element (a witness) and prove P(witness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a concrete expression for the witness (often built from givens) and justify it satisfies the required property. Example: when proving ∃j∈Z(x^2=2j), set j = 2k^2 or similar as derived from earlier equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existential givens by instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a given ∃x P(x), immediately instantiate it by introducing a fresh name for some object satisfying P(x) (e.g., let x0 be such that P(x0)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is existential instantiation: introduce a new variable and add the instantiated facts to your givens. Be careful to use a fresh variable name to avoid confusion with other bound variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reusing bound variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: When an existential given uses a bound variable name, do not reuse that same name for a witness in a different existential goal — pick a new symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a given used k, and you later need to prove ∃j..., pick j rather than reusing k. This avoids variable-capture/confusion in the informal write-up and reflects the logical distinction between different bound occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove conjunctions by proving each conjunct
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form P ∧ Q: prove P and prove Q separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat P∧Q as two separate subgoals. In a write-up you may split into two paragraphs or steps, each concluding one conjunct, then assert the conjunction. Example: to prove x∈B∧x∉C, show x∈B and x∉C independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conjunctive givens by splitting them
rubrics_metrics.description: To use a given of the form P ∧ Q: treat it as two separate givens P and Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add both P and Q to your list of available facts; use either one as needed. Example: from x∈A∧x∉C conclude x∈A and x∉C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove biconditionals by proving both implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form P ↔ Q: prove P → Q and Q → P separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label the two parts (→ and ←) and give separate arguments. You may sometimes present the argument as a string of equivalences when the two directions are the same steps in reverse (see 'strings of equivalences' rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use biconditional givens by splitting into implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To use a given of the form P ↔ Q: treat it as two givens P → Q and Q → P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add both implications to your available facts and use whichever direction is needed in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strings of equivalences as a proof shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: If the steps used to prove P → Q are the reverse of those proving Q → P, you may present the proof as a string of equivalences P iff R iff Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an abbreviation for proving P ↔ R and R ↔ Q. Do not start a proof by asserting P ↔ Q without justifications; each equivalence in the chain must be justifiable. Example: transforming x∈A∩(B\C) through equivalent membership statements to reach x∈(A∩B)\C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equalities by proving two subset inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A = B: prove A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A (equivalently show ∀x(x∈A ↔ x∈B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common strategies: introduce arbitrary x and prove the biconditional membership statement, or prove each subset inclusion separately. Often use elementwise reasoning and logical expansions of set operations (e.g., x∈A∩B ⇔ x∈A ∧ x∈B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DeMorgan and logical equivalences to rewrite negations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexpress negative givens or goals using DeMorgan/quantiﬁer-negation laws to obtain usable positive forms (e.g., A∩C=∅ ⇒ ∀y(y∉A ∨ y∉C) ⇒ ∀y(y∈A → y∉C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets you convert negative global statements into implications usable with an arbitrary element. Example: converting A∩C=∅ into ∀y(y∈A → y∉C) to deduce x∉C when x∈A.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a goal is a negation and cannot be reexpressed, use contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the goal is a negated statement and reexpressing it would require the same equivalence you are trying to prove, use proof by contradiction: assume the negation of the desired negation and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove ∀x¬P(x) → ¬∃xP(x) or the reverse direction, use contradiction + existential instantiation. The text uses this for directions of equivalences involving negated quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive for conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional P → Q, it can be helpful to prove its contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is particularly useful when negations or parity arguments are involved (e.g., proving 'if x^2 even then x even' by proving the contrapositive 'if x odd then x^2 odd').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by cases for disjunctive givens
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a given P ∨ Q, use proof by cases: assume P and prove the goal, then assume Q and prove the goal; since the disjunction is known, the goal follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly handle each case (Case 1, Case 2 ...). Cases must be exhaustive (cover all possibilities), but they need not be exclusive (some values may satisfy multiple cases). Example: proving A∪B⊆C from A⊆C and B⊆C by cases on x∈A∨x∈B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a disjunction goal by cases or by assuming the negation of one disjunct
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal P ∨ Q, either break into exhaustive cases proving P in some and Q in others, or observe that P ∨ Q ≡ ¬P → Q and prove Q under the added assumption ¬P (the P-false case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The latter approach reduces the goal to proving Q with ¬P as an extra given; it's handy when proving P is difficult but ¬P leads to Q. The book explains this as the same transformation used for ¬P → Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose cases even if not suggested by a disjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: You may break a proof into cases at any time, as long as the cases are exhaustive; the cases need not be suggested by an explicit given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to analyze parity of x in x^2 mod 4, choose cases 'x is even' and 'x is odd' because those exhaust all possibilities and lead directly to the desired conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a given is a disjunction, use its natural cases to guide proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If a given has form x∈A ∨ x∈B, use the two cases x∈A and x∈B and apply other givens accordingly in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In each case, use available subset/given relations to derive the goal. Example: with x∈A∨x∈B and A⊆C, B⊆C, each case yields x∈C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiate indices and witnesses in family/indexed-set arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with unions/intersections of families/indexed collections, use existential instantiation to pick an index i0 with x∈Ai0 (or similar) and proceed elementwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving B∩(⋃_{i∈I} Ai)=⋃_{i∈I}(B∩Ai) uses choosing i0 with x∈Ai0 when x∈⋃, then showing x∈B∩Ai0 and hence in the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving goals that start with ∃ but a variable is already used, rename bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: If a goal requires proving ∃j ... but j is already used in givens as a particular element, rewrite the existential with a fresh bound variable name (e.g., ∃y) and supply that witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids confusion between the existential bound variable in the statement and the particular element introduced earlier by existential instantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize proofs into scratch work and final write-up; justify each asserted step
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scratch-work to analyze logical forms and plan steps, then produce a final proof that only asserts statements after they are justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin the write-up by asserting the final conclusion (e.g., P↔Q) before demonstrating the chain of justifications. The text shows scratch-work columns (Givens/Goals) used to plan proofs.
